pages.title: Solve a laboratory problem in the right order

blocks.text: A student obtains an impure organic liquid and wants to identify it. A sensible sequence is to purify it, examine composition and then interpret its structure and reactions. A correct reaction name cannot compensate for testing an impure or chemically unprepared sample.

This application unit revisits the chapter through decisions: which physical contrast separates a mixture, which chemical conversion makes an element detectable, and which electron change explains a reaction. Each question requires a reason rather than a memorised method name.

pages.transition: Start with the physical contrast that would purify a solid.

pages.title: Choose a solid-purification method

blocks.text: A product dissolves well in hot solvent but poorly when cold, while an impurity remains dissolved on cooling. Choose crystallisation: dissolve in a minimum suitable hot solvent, remove insoluble material as appropriate, cool and collect crystals. The important contrast is temperature-dependent solubility.

A sublimable product mixed with a non-sublimable solid suggests sublimation instead. These methods are not interchangeable: a non-sublimable product will not be separated by simply heating it as though all organic solids sublime. Product recovery and impurity behaviour must both be considered.
Qualitative means identifying what is present. Quantitative means measuring how much is present. A separation, an identification test and a percentage calculation answer different questions.

pages.transition: Liquid separations depend on a different set of volatility and temperature choices.

pages.title: Choose between three distillations

blocks.text: A volatile liquid with non-volatile impurities suggests simple distillation. Two close-boiling liquids suggest fractional distillation. A high-boiling liquid that decomposes on strong heating suggests reduced-pressure distillation. Steam distillation additionally requires a steam-volatile substance immiscible with water.

The fractionating column provides repeated vapour–liquid equilibration; reduced pressure lowers the boiling temperature; steam contributes its own vapour pressure. These are three different physical reasons for separation, not three interchangeable names for heating a flask.

pages.transition: Extraction and chromatography answer related separation problems in different ways.

pages.title: Chromatography versus extraction

blocks.text: Extraction distributes a solute between immiscible liquid layers. Chromatography distributes mixture components between stationary and mobile phases, separating them because their retention differs. Partition chromatography uses distribution between liquid phases; adsorption chromatography emphasises attachment to a solid surface.

On a TLC plate, spots travel 2.0 cm and 5.0 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. Their R_f values are 0.25 and 0.625. The lower value indicates greater retention under these conditions. Changing the solvent can change the values, so compare samples under the same conditions.

pages.transition: A purified sample still needs chemical conversion before some elemental tests work.

pages.title: A chemical test needs the right ionic form

blocks.text: Covalently attached nitrogen, sulphur and halogens are converted into ionic salts during sodium fusion. Nitrogen may then give Prussian blue, sulphur black PbS or a violet nitroprusside test, and halides silver-halide precipitates after suitable interference removal.

These observations are qualitative, not percentage measurements. Also, a sulphide test is not the same as sulphur estimation through BaSO4: the latter first oxidises sulphur to sulphate and weighs a different chemical product. The oxidation state and sample treatment explain the different tests.

pages.transition: Detecting nitrogen and measuring its percentage are separate tasks.

pages.title: Choose a valid quantitative nitrogen method

blocks.text: Dumas measures N2 after converting nitrogen oxides and removing other gases; wet-gas data require water-vapour correction and temperature/pressure conversion. Kjeldahl measures ammonia through acid consumption after digestion, but is unsuitable for nitro, azo and certain ring nitrogens under its usual conditions.

If ammonia consumes 0.00400 mol of H⁺ equivalents, nitrogen moles are also 0.00400. N mass = 14×0.00400 = 0.0560 g. For a 0.400 g sample, %N = 0.0560/0.400×100 = 14.0%. State acid equivalents clearly to avoid a factor-of-two error with H2SO4.

pages.transition: After analysis, use bond changes to classify the compound’s reactions.

pages.title: Classify what changed in a reaction

blocks.text: CH3CH2Br + HS− → CH3CH2SH + Br⁻ is substitution: Br is replaced. CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br is addition: atoms add across C=C. Under suitable elimination conditions, CH3CH2Br + HO⁻ → CH2=CH2 + H2O + Br⁻ removes H and Br while forming a double bond.

The same substrate can follow different paths under different conditions; aqueous and alcoholic basic conditions need not give the same major outcome. Rearrangement changes group positions or the skeleton. The equation describes the overall change; a mechanism supplies its electron-by-electron explanation.

pages.transition: The same comparison skills distinguish actual isomers from resonance drawings.

pages.title: Distinguish isomerism from resonance

blocks.text: Butane and 2-methylpropane have the same C4H10 formula but different connectivity: structural isomers. Two resonance contributors of benzene keep the same atom connectivity and move only electrons. Turning one drawing around does not create either a new structural isomer or a new substance.

Stereoisomers retain connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement. Restricted C=C rotation can allow geometrical isomerism when each double-bonded carbon carries two different groups. Merely having a double bond is not enough: CH2=CH2 cannot satisfy that requirement.

pages.transition: Electron withdrawal provides a test case for explaining, rather than listing, reactivity trends.

pages.title: Use electron effects to explain an acidity trend

blocks.text: An acid loses H⁺ to form a conjugate base. Electron-withdrawing chlorine helps stabilise the carboxylate anion by induction. Thus more appropriately placed chlorine substituents strengthen the acid: CCl3COOH > CHCl2COOH > CH2ClCOOH, all other comparisons being comparable.

The induction effect is transmitted through σ bonds and weakens with distance. It does not require actual release of Cl− from the molecule. The electromeric effect instead concerns a reagent-induced π-pair displacement; it should not be invoked as a permanent σ-chain polarisation.

When several methods appear possible, ask what evidence would select among them: boiling-point separation, heat sensitivity, water immiscibility, adsorption or temperature-dependent solubility. Explaining why a tempting alternative would fail demonstrates more understanding than naming the chosen method alone.

pages.transition: Let us bring the separation, analysis and reaction decisions together.

pages.title: Reason before naming the method or reaction

blocks.text: Match purification to a physical contrast, identify the chemical form required for each qualitative test, and convert the measured product into element mass for percentages. A sample’s analytical treatment determines what a precipitate or gas means.

Classify reactions from their net bond changes and explain them through electrons. Isomers are distinct arrangements; resonance contributors describe one delocalised species. Preserve conditions, charges, bond orders and assumptions in every comparison.

questions.question: Why choose reduced pressure rather than simply more heat for a sensitive high-boiling liquid?
questions.answer: Lower pressure lowers its boiling temperature, reducing the need for temperatures at which it decomposes.

questions.question: Is a black PbS test the same as sulphur estimation as BaSO4?
questions.answer: No. PbS is qualitative sulphide evidence; BaSO4 is a weighed sulphate product after oxidation in a quantitative method.

questions.question: Which reaction type replaces Br by HS in bromoethane?
questions.answer: Substitution, because the carbon skeleton remains and one group replaces another.

questions.question: Do all alkenes show geometrical isomerism?
questions.answer: No. Each carbon of the double bond must have two different attached groups; ethene does not.

questions.question: Why is CCl3COOH stronger than CH2ClCOOH in the stated comparison?
questions.answer: More electron-withdrawing chlorine substituents better stabilise the carboxylate conjugate base through the inductive effect.

questions.question: A TLC spot moves 4 cm and the solvent front 10 cm. What is R_f?
questions.answer: 0.40. It is a ratio of distances from the same baseline and has no unit.
